extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent applicants / patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners and practitioners on applying the written description, new matter, and enablement requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA and post-AIA) during prosecution, amendments, and reissue. Covers when to object or reject, how to analyze claim changes (broadening/narrowing/ranges/genus/species), and the undue experimentation (enablement) test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 112, para. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure; the written description requirement ensures the inventor had possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence) shows written description satisfied, do not repeat a rejection. If not satisfied, repeat the rejection, fully address rebuttal arguments, and analyze any affidavits. Suggest amendments supported by the original description when appropriate, but avoid adding new matter (see Rasmussen; Hyatt v. Dudas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response to applicant's reply on written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must review the rejection basis in view of the entire record (including amendments, arguments, evidence) before repeating any 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record now demonstrates requirement is satisfied, do not repeat rejection in next Office action. If not, repeat the rejection, respond to rebuttal arguments, and properly treat further showings (including thorough analysis of affidavits). See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to claim scope require original support
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of written description commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow limitations, alter numerical ranges, or use non‑synonymous language relative to the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To comply with written description or to obtain benefit of earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365(c), each claim limitation must be supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of a limitation (broadening by omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting an element that was described as essential or critical in the original disclosure can raise written description problems because the inventor may not have possessed the broader invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims omitting matter disclosed as essential/critical violate the requirement (examples: Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder). Such omissions can also give rise to enablement or 112(b) problems. Compare cases where a shape or feature was not described as essential (In re Peters) and was acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for genus claims (addition of generic claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by disclosure of a representative number of species or other indicia that the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus; a single species may suffice only in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is substantial variation within a genus, describe a sufficient variety of species. Cases: AbbVie (functionally defined antibody genus not supported by one structurally similar species), Enzo (single species may suffice when disclosure indicates inventor invented species sufficient to constitute genus), Rasmussen, Herschler, Smythe, Curtis, Gosteli. Examiner must evaluate whether the disclosed species are representative of the claimed genus; inability of ordinary artisans to predict operability of other species weighs against support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing new elements or limitations (narrowing) not supported by the as‑filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not constitute support for every species. Subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable; each case decided on facts and what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art (see Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Rozbicki, Ex parte Ohshiro, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of numerical range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: New or altered numerical ranges must be supported by the original disclosure; the analysis considers which ranges a skilled artisan would consider inherently supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Original ranges 25%-60% and examples 36%, 50% — a claim to 'at least 35%' lacked support (no upper limit), while 'between 35% and 60%' met the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether disclosure indicates inventors considered the ratio/ range part of their invention (Purdue, Union Oil comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251)
rubrics_metrics.description: No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention; adding new subject matter to abstract, specification, or drawings raises a new matter objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If new subject matter is added to claims, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description). If specification amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, reject claims under 112(a). Examiner should require cancellation of new matter; consider added subject matter in making prior art rejections as applicable (In re Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and procedural handling of new matter objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to new matter in the specification (requirement to delete) are subject to supervisory petition (37 CFR 1.181); rejections of claims are appealable to the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and examiner has both objection and rejection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter present only in claims (not elsewhere in spec)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims filed as part of the original specification are part of the disclosure; if originally filed claims disclose matter not in remainder of specification, that claimed subject matter may be problematic for antecedent basis/support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may need to amend the specification to include claimed subject matter; Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis (In re Benno; MPEP § 608.01(o)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Rephrasing or rewording that preserves the same meaning and inclusion of dictionary or art‑recognized definitions known at filing generally do not constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere rephrasing where same meaning remains is permissible (In re Anderson). If multiple definitions exist and a particular definition is added later, the original application must clearly show intent to that definition to avoid new matter or lack of written description (Schering v. Amgen example renaming 'leukocyte interferon' to 'IFN-(a)' was acceptable as renaming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to correct obvious errors do not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may correct errors if the correction would be recognized by one skilled in the art (In re Oda). Limitations apply for reliance on foreign priority documents unless explicitly incorporated by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function/theory/advantage (doctrine of inherency)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclosed device inherently performs a function, has a property, operates according to a theory, or has an advantage, the application necessarily discloses that inherent feature even if not explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application may be amended to recite inherent functions/properties without introducing new matter. To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must show the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities (In re Reynolds, In re Smythe, Yeda Research, In re Robertson, Kennecott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may incorporate material from another document by reference; incorporated material is treated as part of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter. Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p) for policy. Consider the impact of incorporation on 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre‑AIA 112, sixth paragraph determinations (see MPEP § 2181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The invention to be enabled is that defined by the claims. The purpose is to meaningfully communicate how to make and use the invention to the public. Not required to enable a perfected or commercially viable embodiment. Enablement is separate and distinct from written description; a limitation may lack descriptive support but still be enabled if one skilled could make and use the claimed invention with that limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of enablement — undue experimentation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is evaluated under whether the experimentation necessary to make and use the invention would be undue — the Minerals Separation / In re Wands standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test asks whether one reasonably skilled in the art could make/use the invention from the disclosure plus known art without undue experimentation. Complex experimentation is not necessarily undue if the art typically engages in such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wands factors (factors for undue experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when determining whether necessary experimentation is undue include: (A) breadth of the claims; (B) nature of the invention; (C) state of the prior art; (D) level of one of ordinary skill; (E) level of predictability in the art; (F) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) existence of working examples; and (H) quantity of experimentation needed based on the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all Wands factors together — it is improper to decide non‑enablement based on only one factor. Examiner analysis must consider evidence related to each factor; conclusion of lack of enablement is factual and based on weighing the factors (In re Wands, In re Wright, other cited cases). See MPEP §§ 2164.08, 2164.05, 2164.03, 2164.02, 2164.06 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make the claimed invention (enablement: method of making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must disclose at least one method for making the claimed invention that reasonably correlates to the full scope of the claim; disclosure of other methods is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose alternative methods does not render a claim invalid if at least one method is disclosed (In re Fisher, Spectra‑Physics v. Coherent). For unstable/transitory intermediates, need not teach how to make in stable/isolatable form (In re Breslow). If practicing the method requires particular apparatus or starting materials not readily available, the application must sufficiently disclose them (In re Ghiron, In re Howarth).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the claimed invention (enablement: use / utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of utility that connotes how to use the invention, plus recognition by the art that standard modes of administration are known, can satisfy the enablement/use requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosage or method of use need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation. The applicant need not prove the invention is completely safe. See In re Johnson, In re Hitchings, In re Brana; refer also to MPEP §§ 2107.01 and 2107.03.
